title: Lightning strike: reverse triage
stem: A golf course in a thunderstorm. You are the first doctor on scene with a nurse, an AED and a basic kit; ambulances are 10 minutes away. Three casualties: A, 28, apnoeic and pulseless (bystander CPR for 1 minute); B, 45, confused with fern-like skin marks; C, 60, walking with chest discomfort. Triage and resuscitate.

review.text: The walking patient with chest pain. Your notes let patient C self-evacuate because he walks. After a lightning strike, anyone with chest pain, loss of consciousness or cardiac symptoms needs an ECG and monitoring: tag GREEN at the scene, but do not let him leave.

Fixed pupils. Your notes tag BLACK for prolonged arrest with fixed pupils. After lightning, pupils are unreliable (autonomic effects) and must not be used to stop resuscitation; prolonged efforts are justified.

Why reverse triage works. Your notes say 'apnoea may self-resolve'. It is the other way round: the heart often restarts on its own, but the apnoea persists and causes a second, hypoxic arrest. That is why ventilation is vital.

notes:
Checked against ERC 2021 special circumstances (lightning), the Wilderness Medical Society lightning guideline (2014, updated 2021), and AHA 2020.

Reverse triage: in lightning incidents, patients in cardiac or respiratory arrest are treated first, because those who are moving usually survive and arrested victims have a good chance with prompt CPR and ventilation. Lightning (massive DC) often causes asystole, which may revert spontaneously, but the respiratory arrest continues longer and causes secondary hypoxic arrest — so ventilation is vital; VF also occurs. Scene: the storm is the danger (move to shelter when safe); victims carry no charge and are safe to touch. Resuscitate with standard ALS; prolonged efforts are justified. Fixed dilated pupils are unreliable (autonomic effects) and should not be used to stop resuscitation. Look for keraunoparalysis (transient limb paralysis), Lichtenberg figures, TM rupture, cataracts later, and trauma from being thrown (spinal precautions selectively). All patients with chest pain, loss of consciousness, or cardiac symptoms need an ECG and monitoring.

Differences from your notes: (1) Patient C 'walking → self-evacuate' — with chest pain after a strike he needs an ECG and monitoring; tag GREEN at scene but do not self-discharge. (2) 'BLACK if prolonged arrest + fixed pupils' — pupils are unreliable after lightning. (3) The rationale 'apnoea may self-resolve' is reversed: the heart often restarts; the apnoea persists.
